title: ‘It didn’t make any sense’: Daughter wants answers from Halifax police who fatally shot 64-year-old dad
article: "I really loved my dad."
Five words from a daughter whose 64-year-old father was shot on his doorstep in Dartmouth last month by a police officer.
It made no sense.
Sarah Riche got the news over the phone from her aunt Tammy two days after the shooting. Riche couldn't comprehend what she was hearing. She panicked.
"My mind was racing: I said what was he messed up in? What is going on? What did he do?
"It didn't make any sense to me."
Her father had pointed a gun at a Halifax Regional Police officer, her aunt said. That's what she was told when she was contacted by the force about her father's death.
Terry Riche was shot and killed by a single bullet on the evening of Aug. 27. His daughter wants to know why.

What we do know is that Riche died shortly after the HRP tactical team and armoured vehicle showed up at his home on Carleton Street in Dartmouth. A neighbour said 10 minutes later he heard the gun go off.
"I could hear a dog barking, then I heard what was like a Taser sound, and then someone yelled, 'Get on the ground,' then there was a rifle shot," Mark Worth said.
Riche says her dad wasn't a violent man and that she cannot see him pointing a gun at a police officer.
"My father's not a stupid man," she said. "He knows that if he's going to raise a weapon to an officer then it's over."

Besides, she said, her father had little reason to be so reckless. He had a good job working as a naval engineer with the Department of National Defence in Halifax. His personal life was also in order, she said.

"There's no profile that suggests that my father is a threat to the police and did what he said they did. All his bills are paid, he didn't look like he was struggling to make ends meet ... he was a very intelligent man."
He also had some physical challenges. Her father wore a hearing aid and sometimes walked with a cane.

About three hours after the fatal shooting, Halifax Regional Police issued a brief news release that incorrectly stated that the victim was 59 years old. The release said officers responded at about 8:35 p.m. to a weapons complaint involving a man armed with a gun.
He had barricaded himself in a residence, and police set up containment. According to the release, when police attempted to arrest the man, he confronted them with a gun and was shot by an officer.
It also said the incident had been referred to the province's Serious Incident Response Team for investigation.
Riche wants to know why Halifax officers are not required to wear body cameras that could have provided more clarity as to what happened.

She says she's since been in touch with SIRT's lead investigator Patricia Davis, a former Nova Scotia RCMP officer. Riche said Davis wouldn't say whether her dad actually pointed a gun at an officer that night. But Davis did tell her what allegedly resulted in heavily armed officers ending up at her dad's residence on the evening of Aug. 27.

It began with an altercation with a cab driver. Her dad had left a Dartmouth bar, Whiskey's Lounge, on Portland Street. During the ride back home, he had become agitated by the taxi driver. He apparently began insulting the driver and then refused to pay the fare once Riche arrived home.

She said the cab driver wanted to verify her father's address to alert his boss and colleagues of the incident. Some time after that, her father threatened the driver. The driver reported the confrontation to police. Riche said she asked the SIRT investigator whether her dad threatened the man with a gun but said Davis wouldn't tell her.

The Chronicle Herald contacted Davis to verify these details but she said she couldn't comment on an active investigation. SIRT's interim director John Scott confirmed that the cab driver called the police after an altercation but would provide no other details.

Riche says she's looking for a timeline of events leading up to her dad's death. So far, she hasn't gotten that. But she was told by the SIRT investigator that her father went back into his home after being shot. Then the armoured car plowed into the entrance of the house.
Riche said the SIRT investigator explained this was done to protect police.
"She said the tactical armoured vehicle rammed the house to ensure the safety of the responders."
Sarah Riche has other questions. To start, she wants to know HRP's protocol and procedures for dealing with crisis situations.
"Why did a whole SWAT team show up for this? He supposedly poses a threat but only one person shoots. How do they decide to open fire?"
David Cassels, a former chief of the Winnipeg police department, also wonders whether lethal force was necessary.

"They've gone to a situation where they have someone in a house who is essentially holding himself hostage, so the first thing they should do is nothing," said Cassels. "Wait the guy out and if he comes out with a rifle then with all the equipment they have, the firearms, the body armour, they have (everything) they need to protect themselves."
The retired officer is now the chair of the Coalition for Canadian Police Reform. Cassels and the group is pushing the federal government for national training standards for police officers.

He's advocating for an overhaul in training that includes evidence-based de-escalation. That means, in this case, an attempt to calm the situation while containing the suspect. He says most police departments, including the RCMP, are not training officers in de-escalation strategies and techniques. Rather, he says there's particular emphasis on aggressively responding to crisis situations through control and command techniques and the use of firearms.
"The tendency is to just call out the SWAT team because they think more about controlling this individual and perhaps having to kill him, rather than saving his life," said Cassels.
"The main purpose of why police exist in this world is to protect life and property. While that's the role of the police that's not what's being taught in police training today."
The Herald inquired with the Halifax force about whether the officers that arrived at Terry Riche's house had de-escalation training and what attempts they made to de escalate. We got no answers.

The force would also not respond to other questions about the fatal shooting. Const. John MacLeod, department spokesman, said there would be no comment because the matter is being investigated by SIRT.

Jamie Livingston, a criminology professor at Saint Mary's University, says that the Halifax force has a long history of crossing the line when it comes to use of force. He pointed to its response to a homeless protest in downtown Halifax last August which drew national attention. Dozens of officers roughed people up and used pepper spray while arresting participants at the rally.

"I think there are a lot of important questions that were raised around the appropriateness in which the police responded to that situation, in ways that seem to escalate things unnecessarily," said Livingston. "Particularly in Halifax, there are lots of unanswered questions in relation to police handling of situations that seem to be on the excessive use of force side rather than de-escalation."

For now, Riche is hoping the SIRT investigation will provide answers. There's no timeline for completing the investigation or making the report public. She says if she doesn't get answers she will continue to fight for them.
"I'm not letting it go unless they give me enough evidence to convince me that my father's death was justified," said Riche.
